The complacent Lions reappear as the Swa: Chris Fagan was seething on Saturday night. His team had lost for just the second time since May. They’d lost to a club whose chair had just a few weeks ago declared their season “torpedoed”. But Fagan has been around football long enough not to buy into that. He spent most of the buildup to the qualifying final warning his players and the commentariat that Sydney shouldn’t be taken lightly. Fagan knows his own players inside out, and he knows they’re at their most vulnerable when the task before them seems straightforward. He can tell early whether the imperial Brisbane has turned up, or the complacent Brisbane. He says he can tell by their reaction times, by their energy and urgency at stoppages, by whether his defenders are on their heels or their toes. Sydney had six goals on the board before Lachie Neale had touched the ball, and Fagan’s careworn face said it all.   Related: Sydney blow away shellshocked Brisbane to revive ‘torpedoed’ AFL season    “I’m not sure my players believed me,” he later said. “To be honest with you, I tried very hard this week to convince our players it was going to be a tough game. But somewhere back in the deep recesses of their minds, I just wonder whether they really thought it was going to be as hard as what it was.” Even if they had been switched on, Fagan said, and even if they had been somewhere resembling their best, he wondered whether they still would have won the game. That’s how good the Swans were. There’s been some incredible footballing moments at the SCG: New South Wales beating Victoria in 1990, Tony Lockett’s point after the siren in 1996, Nick Davis’s four goals in the final quarter of the 2005 first semi-final and Lance Franklin’s 1,000th goal. Sydney’s win on the weekend is right up there with any of those.    For all the self-inflicted turmoil and the captain’s rotten luck, there is still considerable spirit and talent in Sydney’s ranks. They won it with no-names and they won it with stars. They won it by nullifying Brisbane’s strengths and they won it by probing their soft spots. At one stage in the final quarter, Charlie Curnow, Errol Gulden and Brodie Grundy were all lolling back on the interchange bench, the most relaxed anyone at the club has looked in three weeks. Meanwhile, players like Harry Kyle, Tom Hanily, Jesse Dattoli and Billy Cootee, with less than 50 games between them, were still harassing and hounding a Lions side who had already turned their minds to next week. Few people in football were under more pressure than Matthew Nicks heading into the first week of finals. And the pressure seemed to come out of nowhere. For weeks, Nicks had been telling us that his team were better placed than the one that finished minor premiers this time last year. Indeed, there’s been a quiet confidence about this coach and this team for most of the season. Sure, there’s always pockets of social media and talkback radio who think the Crows should be a superpower again, and that Nicks should be some kind of Malcolm Blight-like figure. But most see the reality – that he’s had one of the toughest jobs in footy, starting from scratch in the middle of a pandemic; that he took them from 15th to minor premiers in six months; and that the team itself is honest as the day is long.    That’s why, four days out from a cutthroat final, it was so disruptive to have the breathless reporting that he’d lose his job if they dropped the Bulldogs game. Someone was presumably leaking. The club quickly endeavoured to douse the fire, but not entirely convincingly. A few minutes into the final quarter, however, and the rat in the ranks was presumably feeling good about themselves. Adelaide seemingly had control of the elimination final at three quarter time. But the Bulldogs kicked three goals in as many minutes to flip the game on its head. Aaron Naughton hitting the post zapped their momentum, however. It was one of many squandered chances, the majority of which came in the opening 20 minutes. Up the other end, Adelaide’s big men seized their opportunities. Up to that point, the Crows had been kept in the game by their defenders, and Josh Worrall in particular. But in difficult conditions for marking forwards, Riley Thilthorpe, Taylor Walker and Darcy Fogarty stood tall and kicked straight when the game was there to be won. It was Adelaide’s first finals win since they trounced Geelong in the 2017 preliminary final. Every analysis of this final series was predicated on the belief that it was a gift to finish third and sixth, and therefore cop a broken Sydney. There was talk of the soft side of the draw like it was a tennis tournament, and of Brisbane just waltzing to a preliminary final. Now, for the third year in a row, the Lions will have to take the long road home. They have three things going for them that still makes them dangerous – a home final, the potential for two MCG games, and years of evidence that they excel when the blade is pressed hard against their skin.
Brisbane Broncos win NRLW premiership af: The Brisbane Broncos overcame a valiant Sydney Roosters comeback to secure their fourth NRLW premiership with a 22-18 victory in a see-sawing and spiteful grand final marked by sickening collisions and a shoving match at the final whistle. The Broncos were fortunate in having the crucial, match-winning try awarded by the video referee, after Mele Hufanga appeared to be held up by Jasmin Strange and Olivia Kernick. With just four minutes left, the Broncos centre – who was named Karyn Murphy Medallist for player of the match – grounded the ball to push her side into the lead. Although the try was awarded, the slow motion replay was far from conclusive.   Related: Brisbane Broncos beat Sydney Roosters in NRLW 2025 grand final – rugby league live    Fullback Tamika Upton, who has now won five grand finals and scored the Broncos’ first try on Sunday, appeared shocked by the late drama at the final whistle, and swore in the Channel Nine coverage. “Fuck, the girls really put in all season for that,” she said. “We got a bit comfortable at half-time there. The Roosters came back like the champion team they are, but [I’m] so proud of the girls, particularly our young ones stepping up.” The result ended an 18-match winning streak from the Roosters, who had also won their last five games against the Broncos. After a clunky first half, the minor premiers faced a 12-point deficit. But they finally showed life 10 minutes into the second half, when fullback Brydie Parker scythed through the Broncos defence to score a long-range try direct from a scrum play. Corban Baxter engaged the line and found Parker, who jinked around Hufanga, streaked through the backfield and carried Upton over in the corner.    Seconds before, Broncos winger Hayley Maddick was inches away from an intercept that would have put Brisbane up 18-0. But she couldn’t keep control of it, and the midfield scrum flipped the momentum in an instant. Within five minutes, the Roosters were level after Eliza Lopamaua held three Broncos at bay to put the ball down. The Roosters then put their noses in front by a sharp blindside move set up by Destiny Brill and Jess Sergis, and finished by Mia Wood in the corner. They survived a scare almost immediately afterwards, when Broncos centre Julia Robinson picked up a handling error from the Roosters. But the video referee brought play back, much to the frustrations of tens of thousands of Broncos fans who had arrived in time to enjoy their club in both the men’s and women’s showpiece. Those fans were rewarded not long after however when Shalom Sauaso cashed over with nine minutes to go. A failed conversion attempt left the Roosters hanging onto a two point lead, until Hufanga crossed to secure the victory for the Broncos. Roosters captain Isabelle Kelly said she was proud of her team’s effort, despite the result. “When you look at our group and the adversity and the resilience that we’ve built this year with so many injuries to key players, I’m so proud that the score line was like because we just dug so deep and we did everything we could for each other.”    They lost playmaker Tarryn Aiken to a serious knee injury three weeks ago, and suffered a blow before the game had even begun. Winger Taina Naividi ruptured her ACL at Saturday’s final training session, forcing a late change. Wood shifted from the bench onto the wing. But that was not the only late change. Brisbane coach Scott Prince decided to start Brill at hooker and Jada Ferguson from the bench. The move looked a masterstroke 29 minutes in when Ferguson forced her way over from a dummy half scurry for her side’s second try. After becoming coach in 2023, Prince has helped redirect the Broncos back towards the summit of the NRLW. Sunday’s clash also had personal significance, marking 20 years’ since his Clive Churchill Medal-winning performance in the NRL grand final for the Wests Tigers. But his contribution to the Broncos could be even greater. Brisbane’s triumph on Sunday was their first premiership since 2020, and re-asserted their status as the nation’s premier women’s club.
Travball emerges, athletics surges, Bris: The highly anticipated Ashes was quickly torn apart by Travis Head’s cameo at the top of the order that has since turned into a much longer stay. The NRL grand final was another scene for an all-time breathtaking display, as the Broncos joined the AFL’s Lions in making Brisbane the epicentre of Australian sport. Here are our writers’ sporting highlights of 2025. Reece Lightning strikes down the Storm It will be a long time before there is an NRL finals campaign like that of Brisbane in 2025. From an unlikely victory over minor premiers Canberra in golden point, through the dramatic second-half turnaround to end Penrith’s dynasty, to the ultimate destination on grand final day.   Related: Piastri intrigue, Picklum magic and Gout goes global: reflections on a year of Australian sport | Jack Snape    Brisbane’s fightback over favourites Melbourne to win the Broncos’ first NRL premiership in 19 years was improbable by itself, but for it to cap off a snowballing run of finals comebacks was fairytale material. Central to it all was Reece Walsh, the electric yet unpredictable fullback who until those few weeks in spring was more potential than proof. Fans thought they had already seen the greatest grand final performance possible. Two years ago Nathan Cleary single-handedly wrested the premiership trophy from the hands of Walsh and his teammates with 14 of rugby league’s finest minutes. But against the Storm, Walsh was everywhere. His brilliant first-half try, three try assists and defensive deeds marked a display few would disagree was the best ever – and in a contest not decided until the final minute. Then Melbourne leaked through the Brisbane line, threatening to snatch victory with a two-on-one. There again was Walsh, Reece Lightning, the Southport plumber. King Walshy, proclaimed on this day. Jack Snape    Sprinters surge on to global stage There is the curiously familiar running stride and mesmerising smile. The viral videos and celebratory selfies. The sold-out athletics meets that live up to the hype. The rapid rise of teenage sensation Gout Gout has brought Australian eyeballs back to the track. It has quickly sparked the imagination for what might be possible for homegrown sprinters at the Brisbane Olympics in 2032.   Related: Gout Gout turns 18 as whirlwind year ends amid high hopes for even faster 2026 | Jack Snape    The sprint prodigy, who turned 18 this week, continued to break records and soon outgrew junior events this year. He completed high school and at the same time found time to train with sprint royalty and formally announce himself to the world. A 200m semi-final berth in his first senior world championships in Tokyo confirmed Gout’s place as athletics’ – and, arguably, Australian sport’s – breakout star. Then there is Lachlan Kennedy, who upstaged Gout in his pet event over 200m at a meet in Melbourne early in the year. The 22-year-old sprinter had earlier won silver over 60m at the world indoors, and later became only the second Australian to run a legal 100m in under 10s. Kennedy missed the world championships due to a back injury, but looms as Gout’s greatest rival on home turf as the duo appear set to push each other further – and faster – for years to come.    Australia’s fastest woman, Torrie Lewis, also stepped up on a global stage. The 20-year-old broke her own 100m national record and set a 200m personal best when reaching the semi-finals in both events at the world championships. Gout is undeniably the shooting star of Australian athletics. But he is far from alone. Martin Pegan Lions roar as modern dynasty beckons I don’t know a lot about hip-hop but when Snoop Dogg walked out on the MCG with a golden microphone and a marching band, I suspected it would be an AFL grand final to remember. Geelong were favourites to win. They hadn’t lost since July and convincingly beat Brisbane three weeks earlier. The Cats’ skill, experience and polish would surely overcome the younger Lions. The first half was neck and neck. But then Jeremy Cameron broke his arm in a clash with teammate Patrick Dangerfield. The Lions got stronger as the game went on, running the Cats into the ground to claim back-to-back premierships. A modern Brisbane dynasty beckons.    Like many Melburnians, I watched the game on TV with friends, including an avid Lions fan, Tash, who grew up in Brisbane supporting the Bears before they merged with Fitzroy in 1996. “Some of my first childhood memories are watching the Bears play at the Gabba and marvelling at how giant the players seemed from the grassy sidelines,” she says. “My family were lucky enough to see the Lions win their first grand final at the MCG in 2001. So when the siren sounded this year, more than 20 years later, even though we weren’t there, that was special.” Rick Goodman Travball beats England at their own game Had Usman Khawaja not holed out on 82 and missed out on completing the ultimate revenge ton in Adelaide, this entry might look a bit different. As it is, nothing on the cricket pitch, or arguably on any sporting field in 2025, compared with Travis Head’s barnstorming, series-defining century in Perth.   Related: Does Travis Head’s knock deserve to be among the greatest Ashes innings? | Martin Pegan    England’s Bazballers arrived in Australia espousing their great entertainment project, and the swashbuckling but surely now doomed philosophy played its part in an enthralling day and a half of cricket before Head came to the crease for a second time. By then, 30 wickets had already fallen, and just 468 runs scored. With England arguably on top in the helter-skelter match and sensing blood, Head, either bravely or stupidly, put his hand up to open in the absence of the injured Usman Khawaja. But with the pressure on, the moustachioed man from the northern suburbs of Adelaide made light of it, and quickly justified his decision. No fear, no hesitation, Head took the game to England, smashing everything the tourists threw at him to all parts of the ground – fittingly by the end, his wagon wheel resembled an exploding firework. The way the packed house saluted their latest hero, both on reaching the milestone and then as he eventually departed for 123, spoke to the magnitude of his thrilling knock.     Head had taken on England at their own game and won. Travball was born and the tone for the rest of the series had been set. Mike Hytner Mitch Brown’s bravery offers a turning point A dark on-field moment was followed by a hopeful one away from the action that helped reveal the highs and lows that sport can bring us, far beyond the wins and losses.   Related: Mitch Brown’s coming out shows the AFL what courage and grace look like | Jonathan Horn    While the football world waited with impatience for the AFL to hand down its sanction to Adelaide’s Izak Rankine for using a homophobic slur during a game, I, like many others, became increasingly furious. First, that the incident happened, that its awfulness was compounded by the league’s lumbering response, and that so many in footy still don’t – or won’t – see the problem. Then, a week later, Mitch Brown became the first AFL player, past or present, to come out publicly as bisexual, and the experience was the polar opposite to what had come before. The former West Coast player told his story and footy’s carefully constructed wall of indifference came crashing down. While Brown shared some of the horrible things he witnessed as an AFL player, his message was resoundingly hopeful. In the context of Rankine’s slur and the surrounding vitriol of the preceding week, Brown’s courage was immeasurable, and so too was the joy and strength he allowed others to take from his words. I wish this wasn’t a moment of such significance. But because of the culture of homophobia in men’s footy, it is. Brown’s decision – and bravery – to speak publicly may be the turning point that the sport so desperately needed. Jo Khan
Gina Rinehart lobbied for controversial: Australia’s richest person, Gina Rinehart, lobbied for controversial plans to host 2032 Olympic rowing events on the Fitzroy River at Rockhampton, documents released by the Queensland government show. The plans to send rowers 600km north of host city Brisbane – to a river that is natural habitat for saltwater crocodiles, and which prompted significant backlash among the rowing and broader Olympic communities – were announced by the Queensland government in March last year. The newly elected Queensland government conducted a venues review that was finalised in early 2025.   Related: Can crocodiles and canoeists coexist at Australia’s 2032 Olympic Games?    It used the review process to justify breaking election promises not to build a new stadium. But the decision to send rowing events to Rockhampton went against the review’s recommendations, which suggested rowing be relocated to Sydney and held at the existing facility near Penrith. Concerns about the Fitzroy River’s suitability go well beyond the most glaring reason – the saltwater crocodiles, which are occasionally found in the water at Rockhampton, which sits just above the Tropic of Capricorn.    International and Australian rowing officials and competitors have raised various concerns, including that a rowing facility built in Rockhampton would become a “white elephant”. There are also concerns any potential course would not it meet the strict technical requirements for international racing regarding weeds, water quality and currents. An undated letter from Rinehart to Bleijie obtained by Brisbane Times, but understood to have been sent prior to the government’s decision to move rowing to Rockhampton, lobbies for the relocation of rowing to central Queensland. Rinehart, a key financial backer of the rightwing One Nation party, and who has extensive mining and pastoral interests, says in the letter that hosting an Olympic event in the “beef capital” would “enable Queensland to tell the iconic Australian story of our pastoralists and farmers”. “As a supporter of Australian rowing for more than a decade, I am aware that the Australian team often trains on the Fitzroy River and that Rockhampton annually hosts the Queensland state school championships,” Rinehart said.“This rowing facility is world class and is already close to major infrastructure, so it offers the potential to save taxpayer money. “As you would know too, Rockhampton has also always been a major mining town, the nearby Mt Morgan mine was once the biggest gold mine in the world. “I am told that metals from this mine will produce the gold, silver, and bronze medals for the Olympics! To marry showing where the Olympic medals come from and having Olympic events nearby, sounds to me like a beautiful extra!” A statement from a Hancock Prospecting spokesperson released late on Thursday said Rinehart was a supporter of Australian athletes and rejected any suggestion there might be an “ulterior motive” for her to write the letter. “Mrs Rinehart has also for decades been a huge champion of regional Australia and her insights expressed in the letter were done so for the reason of outlining the benefits hosting Olympic events would bring to a regional town like Rockhampton. “Too often regional towns are forgotten.”
Queensland state budget 2025: LNP to boo: The Queensland Liberal National party’s first state budget in a decade will grow the size of the public sector, increase government spending and entrench deficits for the foreseeable future. The treasurer, David Janetzki, said his “no austerity” budget – the first by the state’s conservatives since Campbell Newman lost power in 2015 – sought to end “scare campaigns” about his party’s record of job cuts and asset sales. In the process, the state’s total debt is now projected to top $200bn for the first time. Ratings agency S&P said the budget “highlights a sharp deterioration in the state’s finances”. An S&P bulletin warned on Tuesday that its credit rating for the state, currently at AA+ for long-term debt, “remains elevated”. Among the announcements is the introduction of a home equity scheme that would allow first home buyers earning up to $150,000 a year to buy a home with a 2% deposit. The government will also continue to fund many of the cost-of-living relief measures introduced under Labor, including 50c public transport fares, sports vouchers and energy rebates. The LNP had campaigned on promises not to cut these programs and has had to find additional money to keep the cheap fares permanently. Janetzki said Labor had “cheapened the budget papers last year to nothing more than an advertising hoarding”. “The adults are back,” he said. Queensland’s operating deficit for 2025-26 is set to top $8.6bn, up from the $5.4bn expected. The budget papers warn of a likely downgrade by ratings agencies as a result of the state’s worsening fiscal condition: “A long-term deterioration of Queensland’s fiscal position has increased the likelihood of further heightened interest payments across the foreseeable future.”   Related: Queensland budget 2025: Crisafulli vows no austerity despite state facing $218bn debt    Janetzki said: “We’re being squeezed on revenues. GST and coal royalties. We’re going to apply expense discipline in the years ahead.” He said state debt, on track to hit $205.7bn over the forward estimates, was lower than had been predicted under Labor. That figure is disputed: it comes from a mid-year update delivered by the new government taking into account its claims that Labor had hidden “vast and broad” cost blowouts that had not been on the books. Compared with Labor’s 2024-25 budget, debt is now forecast to be higher across the forward estimates. The premier, David Crisafulli, and Janetzki told reporters there had been a need to increase frontline staffing levels, spending and debt to repair service delivery problems – particularly in relation to health, youth justice and policing – that had emerged under Labor. “We are front-loading investment into jobs and services,” Janetzki said. “Through the calm and methodical approach we’ve taken, we have laid down a path to surplus.” With the 2032 Olympic Games on the horizon, the government has allocated $950m over four years for the construction of an athletes’ village, and $864m for “the first minor venues projects approved for procurement”. The centrepiece announcement of budget day was a shared equity scheme for 1,000 first home buyers, covering homes up to $1m. Requiring just a 2% deposit, Janetzki called it the “most generous in the country”. He rejected suggestions this could lead new buyers into mortgage stress. The parents of every primary school-age child will also receive $100 from 1 January next year. That comes on top of an existing $200 rebate for children’s sports costs. The last time an LNP government delivered its first budget, the former premier Campbell Newman announced the sacking of 14,000 public sector workers. Under Janetzki, the headcount increases by 6,073. Most of these new workers – about 4,700 – will be within the health service. There will also be additional hiring in the Department of Education and the Queensland police service. But wages look to be likely to stall, triggering a likely fight with public sector unions who are pushing for a better pay offer. Employee expenses, the largest expense category, are contained to a “more sustainable average annual rate of 3.5 per cent” for the four years after 2025-26, according to the budget. That figure includes both headcount and wages. The government has offered an increase of 3% next year and 2.5% for the following years.

A fake website and a deluge of CVs: the: When the first emails arrived, they were easily dismissed as spam. But as strangers continued to boast about their defence and security credentials, they became impossible to ignore. From mid-2025, a small Australian consultancy firm called Horizzen started receiving emails and strange calls from people applying for vague jobs in the United States. It would have been an ambitious global expansion for the Brisbane-based firm, which only had a few domestic clients. Except, it wasn’t hiring.   Related: A bungled bomb plot in Poland exposed a spy – but whose spy was he?    Without its knowledge, a fake consultancy firm impersonating Horizzen had been launched online. It claimed to be an “architect of influence” and was overseeing a recruitment blitz for experts in defence, trade and politics. “It was using our company name, business address, phone number and content, but with a different design,” a Horizzen spokesperson said. “At first, I dismissed it as a cheap knock-off.” Some determined jobseekers, eager to impress, also sent their detailed CVs and cover letters to Horizzen’s Australian email address. They had been deceived into thinking they were the same organisation. In June – one year after the emails first arrived – Horizzen realised the scale of deception. The website falsely assuming its identity had been seized by the US Department of Justice, as part of an ongoing multi-agency investigation into alleged Chinese espionage.    The company had been drawn into what western intelligence agencies allege is a systematic campaign by Chinese spies to recruit and pressure people into revealing valuable secrets. Websites used to ‘trick, recruit, coerce’ In early June, Australia’s domestic intelligence agency joined counterparts in the UK, US, Canada and New Zealand to issue a rare public warning. They were convinced that Chinese spies were running fake consultancy firms and posing as recruiters on platforms such as LinkedIn. The intelligence services alleged that successful job applicants were tested for their knowledge of key issues, and then paid for reports. Eventually, the fake firms would push for “more privileged information” and switch to encrypted messaging services. “Chinese intelligence officers pose as online HR recruiters or consultants who represent fake, but often legitimate looking ‘cover companies’ and claim to be located in countries outside China,” the joint Five Eyes statement said. Within 24 hours of that warning, the FBI obtained a warrant to seize the website impersonating Horizzen. It also shut down another 12 websites accused of targeting US citizens who have valuable knowledge. One allegedly belonged to a fake consultancy firm that was pretending to be based in Western Australia, a US court heard. Job adverts for the company were allegedly posted by someone based in Thailand. A LinkedIn profile for the consultancy firm remains online today, but claims its office is in Melbourne.   Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email   In an affidavit provided to the court, a senior FBI officer alleged all 13 seized websites were created to “recruit individuals in the United States to obtain sensitive and possibly classified information in exchange for monetary payments” on China’s behalf. The FBI agent told the court that the websites used a mixture of aliases, stolen identities and AI-generated photographs to deceive applicants. According to the FBI, the consultancy firm pretending to be Horizzen told recruits they would “establish a formal relationship” with another consultancy firm, called Catalyst Global Solutions (CGS), whose website was also seized by the FBI. CGS’s website and job adverts claimed it was “among DC’s top firms”, despite having a listed address in Lahore, Pakistan.    And, according to the FBI, CGS used an Australian job website to recruit analysts and consultants who specialised in “international relations” and “geo-politics”. In at least one case, it is accused of directly seeking an expert in the Indo-Pacific region. It is unknown whether they succeeded. When the 13 websites were seized, Roman Rozhavsky, the FBI’s assistant director responsible for counter-intelligence, alleged they “illustrate the lengths the Chinese government’s intelligence services will go to as they try to use AI-generated content to trick, recruit, or coerce”. That claim has been flatly rejected by the Chinese embassy in Canberra. An embassy spokesperson told Guardian Australia: “The US accusation has no factual basis and is purely smears and denigration. “China firmly opposes this.” ‘Shock and disbelief’ In Brisbane, confirmation of the FBI’s investigation left the small team at Horizzen stunned. “My first reaction was shock and disbelief,” the company spokesperson said. “What is the reputational damage to the company and other people who may have been misled?” Horizzen believes its identity was deliberately copied by the fake consultancy firm to make it appear authentic, trusted and long-established. “I cannot say who created it or what they intended, but the extent of the copied information makes coincidence very difficult to accept,” a spokesperson said. “It clearly shows that identity theft can happen to any legitimate businesses.”    The FBI has accused those websites of deliberately obscuring their true location to deceive applicants. It told a US court the website impersonating Horizzen has been registered in India. “While we cannot comment on an ongoing investigation, the FBI is aware that malicious online actors often use ‘spoofing’ or other techniques to appear legitimate when targeting innocent people and businesses,” an FBI spokesperson told Guardian Australia. The Australian Security Intelligence Organisation did not comment on Horizzen’s experience, but has repeatedly warned of similar espionage activity. In 2024, Asio alleged a spy ring known as “the A team” was targeting Australians with access to privileged information on LinkedIn. “The spies pose as consultants, headhunters, local government officials, academics and thinktank researchers, claiming to be from fictional companies,” Asio’s annual threat assessment said. ‘Frightening scale’ While the suspicious emails and calls to Horizzen’s team have stopped, they remain concerned their experience may be increasingly common. Like the FBI, they worry that rapid developments in artificial intelligence are making it easier for malicious actors to deceive innocent people. “My experience shows that online impersonation can be far more serious than it first appears,” the spokesperson said. “Whether or not AI was used in this case, AI gives opportunists the ability to create convincing websites, communications, images and corporate identities quickly, cheaply and at frightening scale.” Five Eyes intelligence agencies are urging anyone who believes they have communicated with a suspicious consultancy firm or recruiter to report all details of their interaction. “Ensure you disengage from the profile and don’t interact any further,” Asio’s official guidance says. In Brisbane, Horizzen is urging people not to ignore any suspicious activity. “Businesses and individuals need to take unexpected approaches, strange websites and apparent impersonation seriously, because what looks like ordinary spam may be connected to something far more sinister,” the spokesperson says.

The first thing is the noise – chopper blades cutting through the air as helicopters come and go from the main army response centre, at the entrance to Nepal’s flood zone.
Then, there is the smell. A putrid, iodine smell. Blood and bone. The severe heat beating down on bodies packed into white bags – being carried off helicopters and laid in an area so families can identify them.
On Sunday the combined toll in Nepal and Tibet climbed to 781 dead and more than 3,000 people missing. Forty-three of them are Australians. The humanitarian crisis on the ground is huge – but aid, a large amount of it from Australia, has started to arrive.
An additional $3m, on top of $5m already announced, was confirmed on Monday morning.
The army barracks have become the heartbeat of the crisis – bringing survivors in, taking supplies out and trying to place the dead with their families, so they can be laid properly to rest.
“With every helicopter there are mixed feelings,” says Plan International’s Unni Krishnan, who is on the ground in the Nuwkot district to oversee the response.
“It’s a scene of hope and despair – there are families here who have been waiting for three days to hear about their loved ones … Some of them will arrive and some of them will not.”
Outside the army barracks, the single road entering Nepal’s flood zone was busy on Sunday. While family members gather outside the gates, waiting for news, huge parcels of supplies are making their way up the valley. The response is still in crisis mode – focused on clean water, enough food and shelter.
“We’re seeing the true nature of the floods,” Krishnan says. “It’s reconfigured landscapes and lives.
“Homes are destroyed. We can see spaces, doorways, where barely a cat or a dog could get through now, where people used to walk through. It’s all gone.”
‘It was seconds’
Plan International are part of the massive coalition of Australian charities operating under the Emergency Action Alliance to deliver urgent relief. On Sunday evening, the Australian government tipped another $1m into the hat, bringing the total amount, including public donations, to $3.8m.
Getting the basics in is hard. Huge trucks have dropped supplies off at the beginning of the flood zone, where they are kept in makeshift storerooms. The next day it can be picked up by smaller 4WDs and taken up the valley.
The government is tightly controlling what goes where. After the 2015 earthquake, where the response was rapid but disorganised, communities were forced to bury non-essential items, so international charities are not allowed to distribute things themselves. When aid reaches an area, it’s registered with an official, who then distributes it.
Workers have been able to reach the worst-hit district, Rasuwa, but have not been able to get as far as the border checkpoint, where many of the missing Australians were last heard from.
One aid worker in Bidur, who was not cleared to speak to the media, says his colleagues who had managed to get up the valley had estimated that as many as 70% of the people living there were lost.
“Because down here they had warning, maybe 10-15 minutes,” he says. “But up there it was seconds. So there will be bodies trapped in the mud, that will be difficult to identify and difficult to rescue. And the smell, the smell.”

 
  
   
    
   
  
 

Another worker says the people who survived the floods have moved up on to the hills – staying in makeshift relief centres or with relatives. Many of the villages have been cut off completely. In Bidur, hundreds of people are stuck on the wrong side of the river after the bridge was washed away. There is a market but, once they eat through the supplies left, the only option will be aid drops by helicopter.
On Sunday night, hundreds of people gathered across Australia to hold candlelight vigils for Nepal. The connection between the two countries runs deep – there are 200,000 Nepalese diaspora living in Australia.
‘Namaste’
Here, on the other side of the world, the connection cuts through the tragedy.
Bhagat Lal, 68, is sitting outside his house just 100 metres away from the river. He hears an Australian accent and launches into a greeting: “Namaste,” he says.
One of his sons is studying in Brisbane. Although they have family missing, his son will stay in Australia until they have more information. Through a translator, Lal explains how his relatives, two mothers and two children, are missing. Their whole house was found washed up on the bank of the river, 100 metres from where they lived.
“From the ground level, the river was flowing nine, 10 metres high,” Lal says. “It shook the house … the house got carried 100 metres away.”

 
  Me and my husband grabbed our children in our arms, and we just ran
  
   Sulochana Tamang
  
 

After the aid trucks are emptied, the Plan International team head up the hill to the relief centre, where they are dropping off a water tank.
The centre has become home for 92 displaced Nepalese; 53 of them are children. A worker from the centre points to one young boy – both his parents are gone. The girl next to him: no one knows where her mother is, but her father is here.
Many of them are from the Rasuwa district. Some were found by the Nepalese army; others walked. One group of children, some dressed in their school uniforms, walked for more than six hours to get to Bidur.
They sleep on the floor in large shared rooms, or on makeshift hospital beds that have been brought in. Lunch is served – noodles and veggies. Some of the kids are given haircuts. Their days are spent sitting in the shade or running around with the dogs. Others wrap themselves fully in blankets, lying inside, their heads covered from the world.
‘Everything is gone’
Sulochana Tamang, 30, is staying at the centre. She was rescued from the side of a mountain, her two children aged seven and two, in her arms.
“My town is on the border of Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts,” she says through a translator.
“When the flood came, me and my husband grabbed our children in our arms, and we just ran. We fled up the mountain.”
After two days, they were found by the army, who helicoptered them to the barracks. The family of four survived, but they have lost relatives. Tamang stares out over the mountains.
“There are around 80 households in my village. Everything is gone. There is nothing remaining.”
Like the others, Tamang will live at the centre, possibly for months. There is nowhere else to go.
Plan are going to bring in learning materials, so the children don’t miss too much of their schooling. They will make sure the food is nutritious and see if they can get Clowns Without Borders over to bring in some joy.
“The scale of the distraction is clearer today,” Krishnan says. “But we are also seeing increasingly how people in Nepal are united and people in the rest of the world are with them.
“The contributions of the Australian public have been a huge boost, because the relief workers are reminded they’re not alone in that crisis.”
